question: How can a generative model that learns gradients of log-densities be used to test whether two variables are independent given a third, while controlling the false-positive rate?
answer: A score‑based generative model learns an approximation of the gradient of the log‑density (the “score”) of a conditional distribution.  By first estimating the conditional score with a sliced conditional‑score‑matching procedure, one can run conditional Langevin dynamics to draw samples that follow the null‑hypothesis distribution \(P_{X\mid Z}\) (and similarly for \(Y\mid Z\)).  These synthetic samples represent what would be observed if \(X\) and \(Y\) were conditionally independent given \(Z\).  A goodness‑of‑fit test is then applied to compare the real joint data to the generated null data; because the samples are produced from the estimated conditional score, the test inherits precise Type‑I error (false‑positive) control.  In this way, the gradient‑based generative model provides a way to test conditional independence while accurately controlling the false‑positive rate【1】.
